validated_results.title: Case-control study of lifetime alcohol intake and prostate cancer risk.
validated_results.reason: Population-based case-control study reporting odds ratios for lifetime alcohol intake and incident prostate cancer, matching the requested nutritional exposure and outcome.

extraction.comparison_type: highest intake quartile of lifetime alcohol intake compared to non-drinkers (non-aggressive prostate cancer)
extraction.population: Men with stage T2 and higher prostate cancer diagnosed between 1997 and 2000 and frequency-matched population controls identified through random digit dialing

sample_size.excerpt: We examined the relation between both current and lifetime alcohol intake and prostate cancer risk in a population-based case-control study in Alberta, Canada with 947 cases with stage T2 and higher prostate cancer diagnosed between 1997 and 2000 and frequency matched to 1,039 controls, identified through random digit dialing.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 947 + 1039 = 1986

cases.excerpt: We examined the relation between both current and lifetime alcohol intake and prostate cancer risk in a population-based case-control study in Alberta, Canada with 947 cases with stage T2 and higher prostate cancer diagnosed between 1997 and 2000 and frequency matched to 1,039 controls, identified through random digit dialing.

effect_size.excerpt: Current alcohol intake did not increase prostate cancer risk but lifetime intake increased risk for both non-aggressive and aggressive cases, with an odds ratio of 1.78 (95 % CI 1.19-2.66) and 2.00 (95 % CI 1.19-3.36), respectively, for the highest intake quartile compared to non-drinkers with evidence for a linear trend.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Current alcohol intake did not increase prostate cancer risk but lifetime intake increased risk for both non-aggressive and aggressive cases, with an odds ratio of 1.78 (95 % CI 1.19-2.66) and 2.00 (95 % CI 1.19-3.36), respectively, for the highest intake quartile compared to non-drinkers with evidence for a linear trend.
